transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Chu (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Nova Finance - Head of ML), Ben Ortiz (Platform), Dylan Park (CTO)

Summary:
Redwood team walked through Optimize recommendations focused on batching and prefix/KV cache tradeoffs for Nova Finance's conversational assistant workload. Discussed cost model assumptions (tokens/s, cache hit rate, batch sizes), latency SLOs, and pilot next steps. Customer raised questions about data residency, encryption/KMS, and benchmarking methodology. Agreed to share cost model spreadsheet and run a focused benchmark.

Topics:
- Workload profile and success criteria
- Batching strategies and latency vs throughput tradeoffs
- Prefix/KV cache design and hit-rate impact on token generation
- Cost model assumptions and end-to-end unit economics
- Dedicated vs hosted deployment considerations, security controls

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samira from Redwood and with me is Ethan, our systems SE. Quick intros?
[00:08] Aisha (Nova): Hi I'm Aisha, head of ML at Nova Finance, joined by Ben and Dylan. We're excited to see the Optimize walkthrough.
[00:15] Ben (Nova): Hey all.
[00:17] Ethan (SE): Hi, quick agenda — we'll cover batching basics, then KV/prefix caching, then run through a simple cost model with numbers you can reuse, and finish with recommended pilot steps. Sound good?
[00:26] Dylan (CTO): Yep, great. We're mostly worried about token costs and tail latencies, also data residency and compliance.
[00:33] Samira: Perfect, we'll call out security stuff as we go. Ethan, want to start with batching?
[00:38] Ethan: Sure. So batching is about grouping concurrent requests into one GPU forward pass to amortize compute. For Nova's conversational flows — you mentioned 10k requests/day and a 200ms P95 SLO right?
[00:50] Aisha: That's right; most requests are short, 40–120 tokens generated. We do have some longer summary calls but those are rarer.
[00:58] Ethan: Ok that shapes advice. Two levers: request batching and continuous batching. Request batching groups ready requests; continuous batching holds a short window (e.g., 5–10ms) to improve batch size. For small seq lengths, moving from batch 1 to batch 8 often gives 2.5–3x throughput improvement.
[01:15] Ben: But that increases latency for single requests, right? Our app needs sub-200ms P95.
[01:19] Ethan: Right — that's the tradeoff. We usually suggest dynamic policies: target latency budget + target throughput. Example: keep immediate mode for requests where user is waiting (chat) and use 5–10ms hold on background tasks or internal reranks. Also predictability matters — Dedicated capacity can keep lower variance.
[01:33] Aisha: Makes sense. How does the KV/prefix cache fit in?
[01:36] Ethan: Great question. Prefix/KV caching avoids recomputing earlier transformer states for repeated prefixes — think system prompts, user profiles, or instruction text. For a chat assistant with common opening prompts, you can cache the KV for the prompt and reuse it across requests.
[01:51] Samira: I'll show the cost model slide — basic assumptions first.
[01:54] Samira: Example assumption set: 10k requests/day, average input 60 tokens, average output 80 tokens. Without caching, that's 10k * 140 tokens = 1.4M tokens/day. If you achieve a 70% KV cache hit on prefixes, it reduces the compute tokens by roughly the cached prefix fraction — in practice we've seen 50–70% net token reduction depending on prompt lengths and hit patterns.
[02:18] Aisha: Wait can you unpack that 70% hit number? How do we estimate it?
[02:22] Ethan: Sure — it's the percent of requests where the prefix KV is already present on the serving node and can be reused. If your flows have stable system prompts and templated instructions, hit rates are higher. We usually profile logs for 2–4 weeks to estimate prefix uniqueness. If you have per-user personalization that changes every request, hit rate goes down.
[02:40] Ben: What about memory — KV caches per model can be large. Does Redwood manage memory eviction?
[02:45] Ethan: Yes, our runtime uses LRU/TTL eviction policies and can be sized per deployment. For Dedicated, you can allocate larger KV cache memory. There's also multi-tenant considerations for hosted — we limit per-tenant footprint. We can estimate footprint: for a 2k-token prefix KV it's ~X MB (model dependent). We'll send a sizing table.
[03:02] Dylan: You mentioned prefix vs full KV — difference?
[03:05] Ethan: Prefix cache stores KV slices for tokens up to prefix length; full KV caching is more aggressive and stores more state across longer sequences — it's a memory/cost question. Prefix is useful for fixed system prompts. Full KV helps when users have long conversation history reused often.
[03:18] Aisha: Ok. Now the cost model — can you run the numbers for our profile?
[03:22] Samira: Yep. Baseline: hosted API price estimate (variable) — for this walkthrough let's use relative numbers. Suppose per-million generated tokens cost on your workload is $X on the hosted model without caching. But for clarity, we'll model compute cost per generated token on GPU.
[03:36] Samira: Example math: assume GPU execution cost = $0.02 per 1k tokens (placeholder; will give exact after bench). 1.4M tokens/day -> 1400k tokens -> 1400 * $0.02 = $28/day baseline. If KV cache gives 60% reduction in generated tokens, new generation tokens = 560k -> 560*$0.02 = $11.2/day. That's ~60% cost reduction.
[04:03] Ben: Those numbers look attractive. What about batching impact?
[04:05] Ethan: Batching reduces per-token GPU overhead; it doesn't change token count but reduces latency per token and cost per token because of better GPU utilization. If batching yields 2.5x throughput efficiency, effective compute cost can drop proportionally — combined with cache you multiply effects. So in our example, after batching you'd see cost drop further, maybe to $4–6/day for the same workload depending on achievable batch size and latency constraints.
[04:28] Aisha: Is that optimistic? Our production tail might not allow large batch windows.
[04:31] Ethan: Right — numbers depend on latency SLO. If you cap the batching window to keep P95 under 200ms, you may only get 1.5x efficiency. We recommend pilot to measure real-world batch distribution.
[04:45] Dylan: Can Redwood's autoscaling respond to bursts? E.g., payroll processing spikes at month end.
[04:50] Samira: Yes — Dedicated has predictable throughput and autoscaling policies with burst capacity. Hosted can also scale but may route to different regions/models with fallbacks. We'll document SLA tradeoffs.
[04:59] Aisha: How do we measure and validate cache hit rate? Do you provide telemetry?
[05:03] Ethan: Yes — Redwood Console exposes cache hit/miss metrics, per-route token counts, KV size, and hit latency. In the Console you'd see per-model breakdown and token-level cost attribution. We'll include a sample dashboard image.
[05:16] Ben: On security: KMS, SOC 2, audit logs — we need encryption in transit & at rest and customer-managed keys.
[05:23] Samira: Understood. Redwood Private/Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and VPC connectors; we have SOC 2 Type II in our compliance pack. We'll attach the security docs. For pilot you can start hosted with logs forwarded to your SIEM, or go Dedicated if you need strict isolation.
[05:39] Aisha: For data residency we need EU region for EU users — is that supported?
[05:42] Ethan: Yes, we have region routing policies — you can pin routes to EU-only hosts or use the Private deployment.
[05:47] Samira: Back to cost model: one more nuance — cache hit reduces forward token compute but you still have KV read overhead and some memory footprint on the serving node. Those are minor compared to full forward pass cost but we'll quantify in the spreadsheet. Also cold-starts reduce benefits until cache warms.
[06:05] Aisha: What about quantization or smaller model variants for cost reduction?
[06:08] Ethan: Another lever — use quantized model variants for background tasks or low-risk routes. Redwood Optimize suggests model variant per-route with auto-fallback. For example, use 8-bit quantized for short completions and higher-precision for long summaries. That can cut compute cost further.
[06:24] Ben: For the benchmark, what do you need from us?
[06:27] Samira: Ideally a canonical prompt set with relative frequency and a traffic profile (qps distribution). If you can provide 2–3 representative flows and example inputs, Ethan can run bench with your token lengths and return latency/cost and expected cache hit rates.
[06:40] Aisha: We'll share that — we need to anonymize PII.
[06:43] Ethan: No problem. We just need pattern shapes, not raw PII.
[06:47] Samira: Let's run a quick hypothetical scenario to be concrete: assume 10k requests/day, 60-token input, 80-token output, 60% cache hit, batching benefit 1.8x given 200ms cap. Baseline cost $28/day becomes with cache $11.2/day, with batching efficiency factor 1.8 -> about $6.2/day. That's ~78% reduction vs baseline.
[07:10] Dylan: Good to show order-of-magnitude impact. We need the spreadsheet to plug in our exact unit costs.
[07:15] Samira: We'll send it. Also, we'll include sensitivity rows: varying cache hit 30–80%, varying batch factor 1.2–3x, and latency budgets.
[07:25] Aisha: Anything else on implementation complexity? We want to avoid major engineering lift.
[07:28] Ethan: Implementation is light if your prefixes are stable: instrumenting the SDK to request cached keys for known prefixes and setting reasonable TTLs. For per-user personalization, you can do a hybrid: cache system prompt and do per-user tokens uncached. SDK changes are minimal — we have client helpers for prefix canonicalization.
[07:44] Ben: Do you have examples of cache TTL and eviction policies?
[07:47] Ethan: Yes: typical TTLs range from 1 hour to 24 hours depending on how often prefixes change. LRU for capacity constraints, and we expose metrics so you can tune. We'll attach a quick config example.
[07:59] Samira: Security note again: if prefixes contain PII, you should redact before caching or keep cache in a private deployment. We'll flag that in the security doc.
[08:09] Aisha: Good point. We'll audit our prompt templates.
[08:12] Ethan: Quick Q/A: (short rapid-fire)
[08:14] Aisha: Does caching change model determinism?
[08:16] Ethan: No — caching only reuses KV states; outputs are identical to re-running prefix each time assuming same model & weights.
[08:23] Ben: How to handle TTL invalidation on model updates?
[08:26] Ethan: We provide hooks so model rollouts can auto-invalidate cache shards or tag caches by model version. Rollouts typically flush relevant caches to avoid stale state.
[08:35] Dylan: Great. Runtime orchestration question — can you route by cost to cheaper model during non-peak?
[08:40] Samira: Yes — routing policies support latency/cost/region as policy keys. You can route low-risk traffic to cheaper variants.
[08:47] Aisha: Any gotchas with multi-region caches?
[08:49] Ethan: Cross-region cache warm-up is a challenge; we recommend per-region caches and warm-up strategies. We'll note warm-up in the pilot plan.
[08:58] Samira: Ok, recap and next steps: we'll share the cost model spreadsheet, security docs, sample sizing table for KV memory, and Ethan will run the bench once you send the prompt set. Pilot plan: 2 weeks of benching + 2-week pilot with monitoring.
[09:13] Aisha: Sounds good. Ben and I will curate the prompt set and confirm timelines.
[09:18] Dylan: Thanks, this was helpful.
[09:20] Samira: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts.
